summary: A key distinction in sacrifice law: communal offerings cannot be 'lost' in the same way as individual offerings. The Yom Kippur goats are communal offerings funded by the half-shekel community fund, meaning they are always replaceable. The HP acts as the community's agent - the entire Yom Kippur service is communal, not personal. This distinction affects all the replacement scenarios discussed in the surrounding Gemara.

learning.ahaMoment: Communal offerings cannot truly be 'lost' because the community always has resources to replace them. The Yom Kippur goats as communal offerings are therefore always replaceable - the community's relationship with God is not contingent on the fate of any particular pair of goats.
learning.memoryAnchor: The community's atonement is never 'stuck': communal offerings can always be replaced, ensuring Yom Kippur always goes forward.
learning.learnerQuestion: In what sense can a communal offering never truly be 'lost' the way an individual's offering can?
learning.coreTension: Individual sin-offerings can be 'lost,' triggering replacement procedures. But the Gemara raises an objection: the Yom Kippur goats are communal. Does the lost-and-replaced framework even apply to them?
learning.coreMove: Communal offerings are funded from the public treasury. The community always has resources to replace them; they can never be irretrievably lost. This structural difference means the entire lost-and-replaced framework targets individual offerings specifically, not communal ones.

takeaway.text: Communal obligations are structurally different from individual ones: communal offerings can always be replaced from public funds, so the 'lost offering' problem is exclusively an individual concern.

learning.learningBlocker: Students may treat 'lost offering' rules as universal. The distinction is structural: individual ownership can be lost; communal ownership cannot, because the public treasury is always available to fund a replacement.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Communal offerings' - you speak of those that come from the terumah of the treasury chamber. 'Communal offerings are different' -
from the New Moon of Nisan onward, they do not come from the old funds. 'In accordance with Rabbi Tavi' -
in tractate Rosh Hashanah (7a). 'New, in its month' - the word 'new' is written repeatedly, in excess,
for exposition, to tell you that there is a month in which you must renew the offerings and bring them
from a new terumah collection; and we derive 'year' from 'year' as beginning from Nisan,
since it is written, 'it shall be the first for you,' etc. 'This works out well
for the goat' - which comes from the terumah of the treasury chamber.
'It is a mitzvah' - and not indispensable. 'The lottery' -
of this year does not designate for the sake of another year.
'And on account of a decree they should die' - said in astonishment: it should suffice
that they graze. 'On account of a sin-offering whose owner died' -
lest the priest die within this year. 'Rather, it is a decree on account of'
a sin-offering that has passed its year' -
lest by the next Yom Kippur a year will have passed
on this goat since its birth, and we hold
that all sin-offering goats are invalidated
after a year, as it is taught in Torat Kohanim
regarding an individual's sin-offering: 'one law shall be'
'for you,' etc. - this teaches that the entire law
is compared to the idol-worship sin-offering: just as that must be within its first year,
so too here it must be within its first year. When it says 'shall be,'
this comes to include the festival goats; when it says
'for you,' this comes to include the idol-worship goats of the individual sinner;
and to include the goat of the prince. 'And we ask: is it itself a decree,'
that it is a sin-offering that has passed its year -
what decree are you speaking of? It is certainly, in fact, a sin-offering
that has passed its year by the following year!
'This is not difficult' - you can find a case where its year has not
passed, in accordance with Rabbi, who says that the year is not necessarily complete
from one Yom Kippur to the next,
since we count by the moon, and the solar year
exceeds it by eleven days, and you must
add to each year its intercalation, the amount by which
the solar year exceeds it. 'As it was taught:'
'a complete year' - stated regarding houses in walled cities, to become permanently the buyer's. 'Rabbi'
'says: one counts 365 days' - whether the court intercalated the year or did not,
for you may count only by the days of the solar year. 'And the Sages say' -
it is entirely as Israel counts: twelve months from day to day, if it is a plain year.
'And if' - the comment is completed on 66a as 'it was intercalated,' explaining that an intercalated year affects the buyer of a house sold with redemption rights within a full year.
